rawInput.complaint:
A 44-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a 5-year history of persistent headaches and nausea. Over this period, she noted progressively worsening vision in both eyes and short-term memory loss. She was born in Honduras and continues to travel there regularly; she has no history of fever, night sweats, weight loss, rash, oral or genital ulcers, or sick contacts. Her past medical history is unremarkable; she does not smoke and has no pets.

On examination, her vital signs were within normal limits. Neurologic examination revealed decreased peripheral vision in both eyes; the remainder of the neurologic and general physical examination was normal. Formal ophthalmologic evaluation showed no signs of ocular cysticercosis.

Initial laboratory studies showed:  
• White blood cell count 7000 cells/mcL  
• Hemoglobin 12 g/dL  
• Platelets 333,000 cells/mcL  
• Creatinine 1 mg/dL  
• Glucose 109 mg/dL  
• Aspartate aminotransferase 111 units/L  
• Alanine aminotransferase 149 units/L  
• Morning cortisol 1.1 mcg/dL (low)  
• Adrenocorticotropic hormone 5.8 pg/mL (low)  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a partially calcified suprasellar and parasellar mass with both solid and cystic components, the largest segment measuring approximately 1.0 × 1.3 cm in the right parasellar region.

cotDiagnosis.reasoning:
The chief complaint is a 5-year history of persistent headaches and nausea with progressively worsening bilateral visual symptoms and short-term memory loss. The patient’s own major concern appears to be chronic progressive neurologic and visual decline rather than an acute systemic illness. The combination of headaches, decreased peripheral vision in both eyes, and a suprasellar/parasellar mass strongly localizes the process to the sellar/suprasellar region, where compression of the optic chiasm can cause bitemporal visual field loss.

Salient positive findings include: chronic progressive course over 5 years; bilateral decreased peripheral vision on neurologic examination; MRI showing a partially calcified suprasellar and parasellar mass with both solid and cystic components; and endocrine evidence of central adrenal insufficiency with low morning cortisol (1.1 mcg/dL) and low ACTH (5.8 pg/mL), indicating pituitary/hypothalamic dysfunction from a sellar-region lesion. Short-term memory loss and headaches are also compatible with a chronic expanding suprasellar mass. Her origin from Honduras and regular travel there are epidemiologically relevant because they raise concern for neurocysticercosis, especially with a cystic/calcified intracranial lesion.

Pertinent negatives are also important. She has no fever, night sweats, weight loss, rash, oral/genital ulcers, or sick contacts, which argues against many inflammatory, infectious, or systemic neoplastic processes. WBC is normal, and the general examination is otherwise normal. Formal ophthalmologic evaluation showed no ocular cysticercosis, which does not exclude neurocysticercosis but removes one supportive clue. The lesion is described as a focal suprasellar/parasellar mass rather than multiple parenchymal cysts, which is less typical for common neurocysticercosis presentations. The chronic visual field defect and central endocrine dysfunction are especially characteristic of a sellar/suprasellar compressive tumor.

The leading differential diagnosis initially includes craniopharyngioma, pituitary macroadenoma, and suprasellar neurocysticercosis.

Craniopharyngioma fits very well because these tumors classically arise in the sellar/suprasellar region and often have mixed solid and cystic components with calcification on imaging. They commonly present with headaches, visual field loss from optic chiasm compression, and pituitary hormone deficiencies. This patient has all of those key features: chronic headaches, decreased peripheral vision in both eyes, a partially calcified mixed solid-cystic suprasellar/parasellar mass, and low cortisol with low ACTH indicating central hypopituitarism. Although craniopharyngioma is often emphasized in children, it also has an adult peak and is entirely plausible at age 44.

Pituitary macroadenoma is also plausible because it can cause headaches, bitemporal visual loss, and hypopituitarism. However, pituitary adenomas are less likely to be calcified and less characteristically mixed cystic-solid with calcification than craniopharyngiomas. The imaging description of a partially calcified suprasellar/parasellar lesion favors craniopharyngioma over macroadenoma.

Suprasellar neurocysticercosis deserves consideration because of her epidemiologic exposure (born in Honduras, frequent travel there) and the presence of a cystic/calcified intracranial lesion. Neurocysticercosis can involve the subarachnoid/suprasellar cisterns and can produce chronic headaches and mass effect. However, several features make it less likely than craniopharyngioma: the lesion is described as a discrete partially calcified mixed solid-cystic mass rather than the more typical cystic parasitic lesions; there is no mention of a scolex, hydrocephalus, meningitic symptoms, or seizures; there are no systemic inflammatory signs; and the pattern of progressive visual field loss plus central adrenal insufficiency is more classic for a sellar neoplasm compressing the pituitary stalk/chiasm. Lack of ocular cysticercosis also modestly weakens this possibility.

Other less likely considerations include Rathke cleft cyst and meningioma. Rathke cleft cyst can be sellar/suprasellar and cause visual/endocrine symptoms, but calcification is uncommon and a mixed solid-cystic partially calcified mass is less typical. Meningioma can occur in the parasellar region and cause visual symptoms, but the cystic component and endocrine abnormalities are less characteristic.

Narrowing to a single diagnosis: the most decisive features are the lesion location (suprasellar/parasellar), imaging morphology (partially calcified with solid and cystic components), and clinical syndrome (headaches, bilateral peripheral visual loss, and central hypopituitarism). This constellation is most classic for craniopharyngioma and is better explained by that diagnosis than by pituitary adenoma or neurocysticercosis. Therefore, the single most likely diagnosis is craniopharyngioma.

Sellar-region mass can cause headaches, chiasmal visual field loss, and low cortisol/low ACTH, but calcification and mixed solid-cystic morphology are less typical than for craniopharyngioma.

Born in Honduras with ongoing travel there and intracranial cystic/calcified lesion raise epidemiologic concern, but the discrete partially calcified mixed mass and classic compressive pituitary/chiasmal syndrome favor tumor over parasitic infection.
Can produce sellar/suprasellar mass effect with visual and endocrine symptoms, but calcification and partially solid appearance are not typical.
Could cause chronic headaches and visual symptoms from parasellar compression, but mixed cystic-calcified morphology and central pituitary dysfunction are less characteristic.
